opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think chain-of-thought is one of those things that's been oversold, at least in terms of what people think it tells us about reasoning. The basic idea is that you give the model examples of step-by-step solutions, or just say "let's think step by step," and performance goes up on some benchmarks. That's an empirical fact, and I don't dispute it. The question is *why* it goes up, and whether it's because the model has suddenly learned to reason.

We looked at this fairly carefully in planning domains like Blocksworld, and also in simpler toy problems like last-letter concatenation. What you find is that chain-of-thought helps when the examples you give are very, very close to the test problems. If I show the model how to stack three blocks and then ask about three or four blocks, it does okay. But as soon as you move a little away, say to more blocks or a slightly different problem structure, the performance falls off a cliff. The model hasn't learned the general procedure from the demonstration. It's doing a kind of pattern matching on the form of the reasoning trace.

And that's the irony. The whole selling point of chain-of-thought is that you're teaching the model an algorithm by showing it the steps. If it had really picked up the algorithm, it should generalize to larger instances. A kid who learns to stack three blocks can stack ten. These models don't. So the human doing the prompting is putting in a lot of problem-specific knowledge, and it's very easy to give the credit to the model when much of it belongs to the prompter. There's a "Clever Hans" element here: the human knows the answer and steers.

My general view is that LLMs are best thought of as approximate retrieval engines, very good n-gram models on steroids, if you like. Chain-of-thought increases the chance that what you retrieve looks like a correct derivation, but nothing guarantees it. The intermediate steps can look plausible and still be wrong, and the model can't reliably check them itself.

So if you want actual guarantees, you need something outside the LLM to verify. That's what we call LLM-Modulo: let the LLM generate candidate plans or reasoning, which it's good at, and have sound external verifiers critique them, iterating back and forth. That's where I think the real progress is, rather than hoping that clever prompting will coax reasoning out of a system that isn't fundamentally doing it.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, chain-of-thought is one of these things where the hype got way ahead of the understanding, and I think we have to separate what it actually does from the story people tell about it.

The story is that if you ask the model to "think step by step," it starts reasoning, the way a person would when they write out the intermediate steps of a derivation. And the anthropomorphic language does a lot of work there. People see tokens that look like reasoning and conclude the system is reasoning. But what we've found, in my group and elsewhere, is that the intermediate text is often not causally connected to the final answer in the way the story requires. You can have a chain of thought that is wrong and a final answer that is right. You can have a beautifully coherent chain and a wrong answer. If the steps were really being used as the basis for the conclusion, you wouldn't see that pattern as often as you do.

The second thing is the brittleness. When you give the model a worked example in the prompt, in-context, it does better on problems that look like the example. But we did this on things like last-letter concatenation and on simple planning problems, and the moment you move away from the exact structure of the example, the improvement collapses. You have to give it a very problem-specific chain of thought to get the gain, and at that point you're basically doing the work for it. You're handing it the procedure rather than eliciting a procedure it already has. A general reasoning ability would not be that sensitive to the surface form of the demonstration.

So my view is that chain-of-thought is best understood as a way of getting the model to generate a longer, more structured prefix that shifts the conditional distribution over the answer. Sometimes that shift is useful. It is not evidence of reasoning in the sense that word has meant in AI for sixty years, which involves something like verification, soundness, the ability to know when you've gone wrong.

That's also why I keep pushing the LLM-Modulo idea. If you want reliable reasoning, don't ask the LLM to be the reasoner and the verifier at the same time. Let it generate candidates, which it is genuinely excellent at, and have an external verifier, a planner, a solver, a model checker, something with actual guarantees, do the checking. Chain-of-thought is fine as a generation heuristic within that loop. It's when people treat it as a substitute for verification that they get into trouble.

And I'd just add, with the newer so-called reasoning models that do long internal traces, the same questions apply. Longer traces and reinforcement from correct outcomes do improve the hit rate on certain distributions. But improved hit rate is not the same as the capability being reliable, and until we have a clear account of why the trace helps when it helps, I'd be cautious about reading it as the model having learned to think.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to distinguish improving performance from demonstrating reasoning. Chain-of-thought prompting can improve performance on some tasks. But the fact that a model produces intermediate steps, and then a correct answer, doesn’t establish that those steps faithfully describe how it arrived at that answer.

The intermediate steps are themselves generated text. They can be plausible, they can be useful, and they can also be wrong. So you cannot simply treat the model’s explanation as a certificate of correctness.

To me, the more interesting question is: can we check those steps? If the model proposes a solution and an independent verifier checks it, then we have a basis for accepting it. The model can be very useful as a generator of candidate solutions without being a reliable judge of its own output.

So I wouldn’t dismiss chain-of-thought prompting. I would resist the jump from ‘this prompting technique improves benchmark accuracy’ to ‘we have established that this system reasons reliably.’ Those are quite different claims.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to separate two questions: does chain-of-thought prompting improve performance on some tasks, and does that establish that the model is reasoning reliably? Those are quite different claims.

Asking a model to produce intermediate steps can help it arrive at a correct answer. But those steps are themselves generated text. There is no guarantee that they are correct, that one follows from another, or that they faithfully explain how the answer was produced. A plausible explanation can make an incorrect answer more persuasive.

From a planning perspective, what matters is whether the proposed steps satisfy the constraints of the problem. If a model generates a plan, we can give that plan to an independent verifier, identify where it fails, and use that feedback to ask for a revision. Then we have something we can check, rather than simply trusting the model’s account of its own reasoning.

So I see chain-of-thought as a potentially useful way of generating candidate solutions. I would be much more cautious about treating it as evidence that we have solved reasoning.
